skills.name: Solve quadratic equations by completing the square

note.text:
Completing the square writes x² + bx + c as (x + b/2)² + something.
x² + bx = (x + b/2)² − (b/2)². Add (b/2)² to make a perfect square.
Example: x² + 6x + 2 = 0 → (x + 3)² − 9 + 2 = 0 → (x + 3)² = 7 → x + 3 = ±√7 → x = −3 ± √7.
Do not forget the ± when you take a square root: both roots count.
If the coefficient of x² is not 1, divide the whole equation by it first.
The completed square also gives the minimum value of x² + bx + c: it is c − (b/2)², reached when x = −b/2.

sections.heading: Your goal and connections
sections.text:
By the end, you should be able to complete the square for x² + bx + c and use it to solve equations that do not factorise, with exact (surd) answers.
Builds on: Lesson {2} (the perfect square (a + b)²) and Lesson {7} (solving by factorisation).
Leads to: Lesson {9}, where completing the square on ax² + bx + c gives the quadratic formula.

sections.heading: Solving with it
sections.text:
Solve {quad(1, 6, 2)} = {0}.
• Complete the square: ({poly([1, 'x'], [3, ''])})² − {7} = {0}, so ({poly([1, 'x'], [3, ''])})² = {7}.
• Take the square root, both signs: x + {3} = ±√{7}.
• x = {-3} + √{7} or x = {-3} − √{7}. As decimals: {roundTo(-3 + sqrt(7), 0.01)} or {roundTo(-3 - sqrt(7), 0.01)}.
If the number in front of x² is not {1}, divide every term by it first: {quad(2, 8, -6)} = {0} becomes {quad(1, 4, -3)} = {0}.

key_words.meaning: writing x² + bx + c as (x + p)² + q
a root that is not a whole number, such as √{7}, left exact
plus or minus: both signs give a root

mistake.why: √{7} and −√{7} both square to {7}. Taking the square root needs ±, or one root is lost.

worked_example.problem: Solve {quad(1, 2 * h, c)} = {0} by completing the square. Leave the answer as a surd.
steps: Half the coefficient of x is {h}, and {h}² = {h * h}.
{quad(1, 2 * h, 0)} = (x + {h})² − {h * h}, so the equation is (x + {h})² − {h * h} + {c} = {0}.

cards.idea: To make x² + bx a perfect square, add the square of half of b.
Taking a square root gives two answers: + and −.

check.prompt: Solve ({poly([1, 'x'], [h, ''])})² = {k * k}. Give the larger root.

misconceptions.explain: Subtract {h} from both sides: x = {k} − {br(h)} = {k - h}.
First take the square root: x + {br(h)} = ±{k}.
That is the smaller root. The larger is {k - h}.

questions.prompt: What number must be added to {quad(1, 2 * h, 0)} to make a perfect square?

misconceptions.explain: Half of {2 * h} is {h}, but you add its square: {h}² = {h * h}.
Square half of b, not b itself: ({h})² = {h * h}.

questions.prompt: Write {quad(1, 2 * h, c)} in the form (x + p)² + q.

misconceptions.explain: ({poly([1, 'x'], [h, ''])})² is {h * h} too big, so subtract {h * h}: q = {c} − {h * h}.
Use half of {2 * h}, which is {h}, inside the bracket.
({poly([1, 'x'], [h, ''])})² already adds {h * h}. Take it away again: q = {c - h * h}.

questions.prompt: Solve ({poly([1, 'x'], [h, ''])})² = {k * k}. Give the larger root.

misconceptions.explain: Subtract {h} from both sides: x = {k} − {br(h)} = {k - h}.
First take the square root: x + {br(h)} = ±{k}.
That is the smaller root. The larger is {k - h}.

questions.prompt: Solve {quad(1, 2 * h, c)} = {0} by completing the square.

misconceptions.explain: x + {h} = ±√… gives x = {-h} ± √…: move {h} across and its sign changes.
(x + {h})² = {h * h} − {br(c)} = {h * h - c}: the {c} moves across with its sign changed.
A square root has two signs: x + {h} = +√{h * h - c} or −√{h * h - c}.

questions.prompt: By completing the square, find the minimum value of {quad(1, 2 * h, c)}.

misconceptions.explain: x = {0} is not where the minimum is. Complete the square: the minimum is {c} − {h * h}.
{-h} is the value of x at the minimum. The minimum value itself is {c - h * h}.
({poly([1, 'x'], [h, ''])})² is {h * h} too big: subtract {h * h}, do not add it.

solution: A square is never negative, so the smallest it can be is {0}, when x = {-h}.
